# Introduction

Understanding what drives community assembly has been a central goal of ecology for a long time [@hillerislambers_rethinking_2012; @diamond_assembly_1975; @weiher_community_1998]. Not taking dispersal limitations into account, community composition is thought to be shaped by environmental constraints, competition, neutral processes, or a combination of all three [@gotzenberger_ecological_2012]. Investigating the functional trait patterns in communities offers insight into the dominant assembly processes at work in a community, and which environmental factors most strongly shape community composition [@ackerly2007; @gotzenberger_ecological_2012]. Environmental conditions are hypothesised to act as a filter, excluding species which may be able to disperse to a site but not survive there [@gotzenberger_ecological_2012; @kraft_community_2015]. This should create a pattern of trait convergence toward an optimum trait for survival [@gotzenberger_ecological_2012]. Competition is expected to promote divergence of functional traits under the theory of coexistence by niche differentiation [@weiher_community_1998]. However, competition may also generate a pattern of trait convergence if species with traits conferring higher competitive ability exclude species with weakly competitive traits [@mayfield2010].

The importance of limiting similarity and environmental filtering in structuring communities are expected to vary along stress gradients. Competition is expected to play a larger role in structuring communities in less stressful or high resource environments, while environmental filtering is predicted to be more important in abiotically harsh environments [@weiher_community_1998; @grime1977]. This idea has been pervasive in community ecology for a long time, but has been referred to as the stress dominance hypothesis (SDH) in recent years [@swenson2007; @coyle2014]. Support for this hypothesis is mixed. For example, convergence of SLA and seed mass increased with elevation in the Gaudarrama mountains [@pescador_spatial_2021], and the assembly of height and leaf area shifted from limiting similarity to environmental filtering with elevation in the Rocky mountains [@spasojevic2012]. However, specific leaf area, stomatal conductance, and chlorophyll content showed increased divergence along the same elevation gradient in the Rocky mountains [@spasojevic2012]. Other studies found no changes in assembly mechanisms along stress gradients, for example, along an aridity gradient in the Atacama desert [@carvajal2023], along gradients of soil water and nutrient availability [@coyle2014], and along an elevation gradient in the Swiss Alps [@scherrer_disentangling_2019].

Micro-environmental conditions are an additional, complex variable that may cause trends in community assembly to deviate from the expectations of the SDH. The importance of micro-environmental conditions in affecting community composition has gained recognition in recent years [@kemppinen_microclimate_2024; @vernham_understanding_2023], but the specific effect on community assembly processes has not been investigated extensively. Micro-environmental conditions may pose an additional filter, selecting species with optimum traits adapted to local micro-environmental conditions [@bergholz2017]. It follows that micro-environmental heterogeneity may promote the coexistence of species with divergent functional traits[@bergholz2017]. Thus, high micro-environmental heterogeneity may generate a pattern of trait divergence, even in stressful conditions. For example, mean moisture and temperature conditions within a 10m transect had a filtering effect on leaf area and plant height, but was related to divergence in LDMC [@stark2017]. Heterogeneity of temperature and moisture conditions within the transect was related to divergence in height and LDMC [@stark2017]. However, many studies find that plant communities follow neutral dynamics at fine scales (refs), or that there is little variation community assembly with micro-environmental variation [@aiello-lammens2017].

Here we will investigate the effect of an elevation gradient (macroclimate gradient) and micro-environmental condition son community assembly in a montane grassland. Macroclimate expected to influence assembly as predicted by the SDH. Micro-environment is predicted to...

Research questions: How does community assembly change with elevation?

Does fine-scale environmental heterogeneity influence community assembly?

# Methods

## Study site

Species composition and functional trait data were collected from three sites spread over an elevation gradient spanning 1000 m: Golden Gate Highlands National Park (low site) at 2000 m a.s.l., Wistieshoek (mid site) at 2500 m a.s.l. and Bokong Nature Reserve (high site) at 3000 m a.s.l (@fig-sitemap). Mean annual air temperature is 12℃ at the low site, 10℃ at the mid site and 7℃ at at the high site. Total annual rainfall varies between the three sites, with the low site receiving 1310 mm p.a., the mid site receiving 1558 mm p.a. and the high site receiving 913 mm p.a. (mean annual temperature and rainfall was calculated as the mean daily temperature and total rainfall between 22/05/2025 and 21/05/2026 measured by the nearest weather stations of the African Mountain Research Foundation). The low site is formally conserved as a National Park where livestock has been excluded, but with large herbivores like zebra, blue wildebeest and eland present at the site. The mid site is situated on land owned by the Batlokoa Royal House and the high site is situated in the Bokong Nature Reserve managed by the National Government of Lesotho. Livestock are not excluded from the mid or high site but were not observed at the sites. Mountain reedbuck, klipspringer and baboon have been observed at the mid site. Grey rhebuck, ice rat and rock hyrax are present at the high site. All three sites were located on basaltic bedrock, and were subject to a similar fire regime consisting of incidental wildfires started by lightning or accidental ignition.

At each site, species composition and functional traits were sampled using a grid design (@fig-sitemap c). Each grid was 8 x 20 m in size, consisting of 160 contiguous 1 x 1 m cells. Eight grids were sampled at the low site, and seven were sampled at the mid and high site (@fig-sitemap b). The grids were spaced \> 80 m apart in each site and were positioned to encompass the full range of environmental conditions at the site, covering a range of topographies and vegetation characteristics. In addition, individual grids were oriented to capture as much local variation in vegetation and topography as possible. This sampling design has previously been applied in high-altitude and high-latitude systems to sample broad environmental gradients and allows the influence of fine-scale heterogeneity to be examined without the confounding effect of macroclimate or species pools [e.g., @mod_outcomes_2014; @momberg_exposing_2021].

Vegetation surveys were conducted in the summer growing seasons between 2019-2023, wherein the identity and cover of each species in each cell was recorded, and a subset of species were measured for functional traits. The functional trait survey collected traits for many species at the two ends of each grid but sampled sparsely in the center of the grid. A species was not sampled for functional traits in adjacent cells. Common species were sampled more frequently than rare species. The following traits were measured (following the standardised methods of @perez-harguindeguy_new_2013: plant height, leaf area (LA), specific leaf area (SLA) and leaf dry matter content (LDMC). Thirty-five percent of species were measured for traits at least once, with these species comprising 87% of the total vegetation cover.

Several environmental variables were measured in each cell of each grid: Rock cover was visually estimated as the percentage of a cell covered by rock large enough to impede plant growth. Soil depth was measured by inserting a metal rod of 60 cm in length into the soil until further penetration was impeded. Soils deeper than 60 cm were assigned a depth of 61 cm. Three soil depth measurements were taken in each cell and the mean calculated. Northness was calculated as the cosine of the aspect of each cell. Slope height was measured as the vertical difference between the highest and lowest point in a cell. Surface heterogeneity was calculated as the standard deviation of elevation in a cell from a digital surface model. The digital surface model was created from drone imagery captured on XX date and... (I probably need to give more info on the imagery here, I will consult with Anika about what is appropriate). Soil moisture was measured in each cell more than 24 hours after the last rainfall event, using a handheld time-domain soil moisture meter (FieldScout 300 TDR; Spectrum Technologies, Plainfield, IL, US) at a depth of 7.5 cm.

The mean soil moisture and temperature of the growing season were calculated using readings from Temperature-Moisture-Sensors [TMS, @wild_climate_2019]. Six or seven TMS were placed in each grid, and recorded soil moisture and temperature readings every 15 minutes for one year (12 January 2023 – 21 January 2024). The start of the growing season was defined as the first day after 21 June when the minimum daily temperature of all loggers at a site were above 5℃. The end of the growing season was the first day before 21 June when all loggers at a site had a minimum daily temperature below 5℃. The growing season was from 23 August to 8 July at the low site, 1 September to 6 June at the mid site, and 10 October to 3 April at the high site. The mean soil moisture and temperature for the growing season was calculated for each logger and interpolated to other cells in the grid. An inverse-distance-weighted interpolation algorithm was used with a power parameter of two. Cells with more than 50% rock cover were not used in the interpolation if they contained a logger and did not receive an interpolated value if they were without a logger. Cross validation showed that the interpolation algorithm could not predict the soil moisture and temperature equally well in all grids (@tbl-validation-results). Although the data is noisy, it still gives an estimate of which cells are wetter or drier than others (I could put a correlation analysis with the instantaneous soil moisture campaigns in the appendix).

A principal component analysis was performed to identify the main axes of environmental variation across the three sites (@fig-environmental-PCA). The following variables were selected to test whether fine-scale variation in community assembly is shaped by micro-environmental variation: mean soil temperature of the growing season, mean soil moisture of the growing season, rock cover, mean soil depth and surface heterogeneity. These variables describe the main axes of environmental variation across the three sites, and may affect community assembly in the following ways: Microclimatic temperature and moisture conditions may differ greatly from the macroclimatic conditions, even in open systems such as grasslands. Different microclimates may act as different filters, selecting for different plant assemblages within short distances of one another [@kemppinen_microclimate_2024]. Rock cover and surface heterogeneity may increase the available niche space, promoting the coexistence of plants with divergent trait syndromes [@vernham_understanding_2023]. Soil depth may be related to higher soil moisture and increased access to resources [@price_within-community_2017], and increased opportunity for underground resource partitioning.

```{r}
env <- read.csv("All_data/clean_data/Environmental data/All_Sites_Environmental_Data_OSF.csv") |> 
  tibble() |> 
  mutate(soil_depth_sd = sd(c(soil_depth_1, soil_depth_2, soil_depth_3), na.rm = TRUE), 
         soil_depth_CV = (soil_depth_sd/mean_soil_depth) *100) |> 
  #variables we are interested in
  select(Cell_ID:row, rock_cover, northness, soil_moisture_adj_campaign2, 
         soil_depth_CV, mean_soil_depth, slope_height) |>
  mutate(mean_soil_depth = case_when(mean_soil_depth > 61 ~ 61, .default = mean_soil_depth)) |> 
  #add elevation variables
  mutate(site = case_when(site == "GG" ~ "low", 
                               site == "WH" ~ "mid", 
                               site == "BK" ~ "high",
                               .default = NA), 
         site = factor(site, levels = c("low", "mid", "high")), 
         soil_moisture_adj_campaign2 = as.numeric(soil_moisture_adj_campaign2))

#import remote sensing derived variables

##Combine all environmental data
all_env_subs <- env |> 
  #join to microclimate indices |> 
  full_join(micro_idw, by = "Cell_ID") |> 
  #join to remote sensing data |> 
  full_join(rms, by = "Cell_ID") |>  
  drop_na() |> 
  select(site, rock_cover:STD) |> 
  filter(if_all(where(is.numeric), is.finite)) |> 
  #3 cells have Inf CV, this is because soil depth is zero, we have to remove them in order to scale
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~as.vector(scale(.)))) |> 
  rename(mean_soil_temp_growing_season = mean_T1_growing_season, 
          mean_soil_moist_growing_season = mean_moist_growing_season, 
          surface_heterogeneity= STD, 
          instant_soil_moist = soil_moisture_adj_campaign2)


all_env_pca <- princomp(all_env_subs[2:ncol(all_env_subs)], scores = T) #not including elevation

###GGplot biplot
env_pca <- ggbiplot(all_env_pca, choices = c(1,2), 
                      varname.size = 4, varname.color = "black", 
                      groups = c(all_env_subs$site)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = all_env_subs$site), alpha = 0.8)+
  scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "grey", "red"))+
  theme_classic() +
  labs(color = "Site")
env_pca$layers <- c(env_pca$layers, env_pca$layers[[2]], env_pca$layers[[3]]) #move the arrows to plot in the foreground
env_pca
```

## Statistical methods

To investigate community assembly along elevation and micro-environmental gradients, I will use a trait-based method which compares observed functional diversity to the functional diversity expected under a scenario of random assembly (following e.g., @scherrer_disentangling_2019; @price_within-community_2017). Rao’s quadratic entropy (RaoQ) will be used as a metric of functional diversity. RaoQ is sum of the trait dissimilarity between all possible species pairs, weighted by the product of their relative abundances. It is calculated as follows:

$$
RaoQ = \sum_{i=1}^{S-1} \sum_{j=1}^{S} d_{ij} \, p_i \, p_j
$$

Where $p_i$ and $p_j$ is the percentage cover of species $i$ and $j$ in a community with a species richness of $s$*.* $d_ij$ is the dissimilarity between each pair of species $i$and $j$ *,* expressed as Euclidean distance [@botta-dukat_raos_2005].  RaoQ was calculated with the FD package [@laliberté2014] using the study-wide mean traits of species.

A null-model approach was used to determine whether RaoQ was significantly different from the functional diversity expected under random assembly [@gotzenberger_which_2016]. Null models are a useful tool to gain insight into community assembly processes, however, they differ in their ability to detect different mechanisms. Thus, an appropriate null model must be chosen to test each assembly mechanism. Here, I followed the recommendations of @gotzenberger_which_2016 and selected the C5 null model to test for environmental filtering, and the C2 null model to test for limiting similarity along elevation and micro-environmental gradients. The C5 null model shuffles the occurrences of each species across cells, such that the richness of each cell, the frequency of species, and species abundance stays the same as in the observed matrix. The total cover of cells, and the identity of species occurring in each cell are allowed to deviate from the observed matrix. Thus, we can determine whether the composition of a cell is random compared to a scenario where species can occur in any cell, after controlling for richness and the commonness (frequency in the matrix and total cover) of species. This null model is appropriate to detect environmental filtering because it allows species to occur in cells where they are not present in the observed dataset and has a low type I error rate [@gotzenberger_which_2016]. To test whether the strength of environmental filtering varies along the elevation gradient, the null model pulled from the entire species pool to fill the null matrix (entire pool model). Thus, species exclusive to one site in the observed matrix could occur at any site in the null matrix. To test whether the strength of environmental filtering was related to variation micro-environmental conditions, we wanted to remove the filtering effect of macroclimate. Therefore, we restricted the species pool that the null model fills the matrix from to the site-level species pool (site pool model). This allowed us to determine whether micro-environmental conditions act as an additional filter after the filtering effect of macroclimate.

The C2 null model shuffles the abundances of species in cells, keeping the richness and total cover of cells constant. The frequency and total cover of species, as well as the identity of species in each cell are allowed to deviate from the observed matrix. The link between a species' mean trait value and its abundance is not maintained in this null model. This gives the model good power to detect limiting similarity, because the competitive ability of species, and thus their abundances, should be linked to their trait values. Thus, one can determine whether composition is random compared to a scenario where the competitive ability of species are not linked to their traits, while controlling for the total abundance and richness of cells [@gotzenberger_which_2016]. The species pool from which the matrix was filled was restricted to the site-level species pool to exclude the filtering effect of macroclimate.

To determine whether functional diversity is higher or lower than expected from random assembly, we calculated the standard effect size [SES, @gotelli2002] of RaoQ as a measure of deviance between the observed matrix and null model. SES is calculated as:

$$
SES = (RaoQ_{observed} - \mu{RaoQ_{null}})/\sigma{RaoQ_{null}}
$$

Where $RaoQ_{observed}$ is the observed RaoQ in a cell; $\mu{RaoQ_{null}}$ is the mean of RaoQ from 999 null models, and $\sigma{RaoQ_{null}}$ is the standard deviation of RaoQ from 999 null models. If SES \>0, functional diversity is higher than expected under null assembly, and it is interpreted as a signal of limiting similarity. If SES \< 0, functional diversity is lower than expected under null assembly, and it is interpreted as a signal of habitat filtering. SES was calculated for plant height, LA, SLA and LDMC, using the C5 entire pool model, the C5 site pool model and the C2 site pool model.

To determine whether community assembly varies with elevation, linear mixed-effect models were used with the SES of each trait from the C5 entire pool model and C2 site pool model as response variables, and elevation as a predictor. To determine whether micro-environmental variables were related to fine-scale variation in community assembly, separate linear mixed-effect models were built for each trait and each site. The SES of each trait from the C5 site pool model and the C2 site pool model were the response variables, and the following predictors were included: mean soil temperature of the growing season, mean soil moisture of the growing season, rock cover, mean soil depth and surface heterogeneity. Predictor variables were standardised to a mean of zero and unit variance prior to modelling. In all analyses, grid was added as a random effect, and a spherical correlation structure was used to account for the spatial autocorrelation between the cells of each grid. To improve the distribution of the model residuals, SES was calculated with the natural log of height, LDMC, and LA in the elevation model, and the natural log of LDMC in the micro-environmental model. Modelling was performed using the nlme package [@pinheiro2025] in R 4.5.2 [@rcoreteam2023].

To investigate the direction in which traits are filtered, the community-weighted mean (CWM) traits of each cell was calculated with the FD package [@laliberté2014]. A linear mixed effect model with grid as a random effect and a spherical correlation structure was used to determine how CWM varies with elevation.

```{r setup chunk}
#import microenvironmental data containing x and y coordinates
pos <- read.csv("All_data/clean_data/Environmental data/All_Sites_Environmental_Data_OSF.csv") |> 
  #variables we are interested in
  select(Cell_ID:row) |> 
  #add elevation variables
  mutate(elevation = case_when(site == "GG" ~ 2000, 
                               site == "WH" ~ 2500, 
                               site == "BK" ~ 3000,
                               .default = NA)) |> 
  mutate(ncolumn = match(column, LETTERS[1:8]), 
         grid = paste0(site, grid), 
         elevation = as.factor(elevation), 
         grid = as.factor(grid)) |> #each grid must have a unique id 
  rename(x_coord = ncolumn, 
         y_coord = row)

#import microenvironmental data containing microenv variables
env2 <- read.csv("All_data/clean_data/Environmental data/All_Sites_Environmental_Data_OSF.csv") |> 
  #variables we are interested in
  select(Cell_ID:row, rock_cover, northness, soil_moisture_adj_campaign2, 
        mean_soil_depth, slope_height) |> 
  #add elevation variables
  mutate(elevation = case_when(site == "GG" ~ 2000, 
                               site == "WH" ~ 2500, 
                               site == "BK" ~ 3000,
                               .default = NA)) |> 
  mutate(ncolumn = match(column, LETTERS[1:8]),  #also add x and y coordinates
         grid = paste0(site, grid), 
        elevation = as.factor(elevation), 
        grid = as.factor(grid)) |> #each grid must have a unique id 
  rename(x_coord = ncolumn, 
         y_coord = row)

#import remote sensing derived variables
rms <- read.csv("All_data/clean_data/Environmental data/Zonal_stats_all.csv") |> 
  select(CELL_ID, STD) |> 
  rename(Cell_ID = CELL_ID)

#import interpolated microclimate indices
micro_idw <- read.csv("All_data/clean_data/Environmental data/Imke_microclimate_indices_idw_interpolated.csv", row.names = 1)


###=========================================###
###Loop to run SES~elevation for all traits####
###=====C5 NULL MODEL, pool = entire========####
###=========================================###
#import SES data
C5_cell_ses_poolentire <- read.csv("All_data/comm_assembly_results/SES_RQ_weighted_cells_C5_entire.csv", row.names = 1) |> 
  rename(Cell_ID = cellref) 

##Combine SES and environmental data
C5_ele_comb <- pos |> 
  #join, one row in env matches many rows in cell_ses due to it containing ses of different traits
  inner_join(C5_cell_ses_poolentire, by = "Cell_ID", relationship = "one-to-many") 
  
#These variables have the best diagnostics
#LA and SLA still have TERRIBLE DIAGNOSTICS
traitlist <- c("SLA",  "log_Height", "log_LDMC", "log_LA")
#lists to store results in
C5_SES_ele_summary <- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist))
names(C5_SES_ele_summary) = traitlist

C5_SES_ele_Rsq<- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist))
names(C5_SES_ele_Rsq) = traitlist

C5_SES_ele_anova<- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist))
names(C5_SES_ele_anova) = traitlist

C5_SES_ele_cld<- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist))
names(C5_SES_ele_cld) = traitlist

for (t in 1:length(traitlist)) {
  modeldat <-  C5_ele_comb |> 
    filter(trait == traitlist[t]) |> 
    drop_na()
  
  
  model<- lme(SES ~ elevation ,
                  random = ~1|grid, 
                  correlation = corSpher(form = ~ x_coord + y_coord|grid, nugget = TRUE), #spherical structure
                  data = modeldat) #only gaussian family possible
  
  #emmeans and letters
  em_model <- emmeans(model, specs = "elevation", type = "response")
  comp_letters <-cld(em_model, Letters = letters, adjust = "Tukey", sort = FALSE)
  
  #Also save results in a list object so we can call it with quarto
  C5_SES_ele_summary[[t]] <- summary(model)
  C5_SES_ele_Rsq[[t]] <- r.squaredGLMM(model)
  C5_SES_ele_anova[[t]] <- anova(model)
  C5_SES_ele_cld[[t]] <- comp_letters
  
}
rm(model, modeldat) #remove to make sure we don't carry the wrong object over

              correlation = corSpher(form = ~ x_coord + y_coord|grid, nugget = TRUE), #spherical structure
              data = modeldat) #only gaussian family possible

  names(C5_SES_microenv_anova)[[l]] <- paste(traitlist[t], sitelist[s], sep = "_")
  C5_SES_microenv_anova[[l]] <- anova(model)
  
  l = l+1

#lists to store results in

names(C2_SES_ele_summary) = traitlist

C2_SES_ele_Rsq<- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist))
names(C2_SES_ele_Rsq) = traitlist

C2_SES_ele_anova<- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist))
names(C2_SES_ele_anova) = traitlist

C2_SES_ele_cld<- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist))
names(C2_SES_ele_cld) = traitlist


for (t in 1:length(traitlist)) {
  modeldat <-  C2_ele_comb |> 
    filter(trait == traitlist[t]) |> 
    drop_na()
  
  
  model<- lme(SES ~ elevation ,
              random = ~1|grid, 
              correlation = corSpher(form = ~ x_coord + y_coord|grid, nugget = TRUE), #spherical structure
              data = modeldat) #only gaussian family possible
  
  #emmeans and letters
  em_model <- emmeans(model, specs = "elevation", type = "response")
  comp_letters <-cld(em_model, Letters = letters, adjust = "Tukey", sort = FALSE)
  
  #Also save results in a list object so we can call it with quarto
  C2_SES_ele_summary[[t]] <- summary(model)
  C2_SES_ele_Rsq[[t]] <- r.squaredGLMM(model)
  C2_SES_ele_anova[[t]] <- anova(model)
  C2_SES_ele_cld[[t]] <- comp_letters
  
}
rm(model, modeldat) #remove to be safe



###===========================================================###
###Loop to run SES~microenvironmental variables for all traits####
###=============C2 NULL MODEL, pool = site====================####
###===========================================================###
#import ses
C2_cell_ses_poolsite <- read.csv("All_data/comm_assembly_results/SES_RQ_weighted_cells_C2_poolsite.csv", row.names = 1) |> 
  rename(Cell_ID = cellref) 


##Combine SES and environmental data
C2_microenv_comb <- env2 |> 
  #join to microclimate indices |> 
  full_join(micro_idw, by = "Cell_ID") |> 
  #join to remote sensing data |> 
  full_join(rms, by = "Cell_ID") |> 
  #join, one row in env matches many rows in cell_ses due to it containing ses of different traits
  full_join(C2_cell_ses_poolsite, by = "Cell_ID", relationship = "one-to-many") |>
  mutate(grid = paste0(site, grid), 
         elevation = as.factor(elevation), 
         grid = as.factor(grid)) |> 
  group_by(site) |> 
  mutate(       #standardise the variables we will use in the model, per site
         mean_T1_growing_season = as.numeric(scale(mean_T1_growing_season)), 
         mean_moist_growing_season = as.numeric(scale(mean_moist_growing_season)), 
         rock_cover = as.numeric(scale(rock_cover)), 
         mean_soil_depth = as.numeric(scale(mean_soil_depth)), 
         STD = as.numeric(scale(STD))) |> 
  ungroup()


###Loop starts here####
#Run the loop for all traits
traitlist <- c("log_LDMC", "Height_cm", "Leaf_area_mm2", "SLA")
sitelist <- c("GG", "WH", "BK")
#lists to store results in
C2_SES_microenv_summary <- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist) * length(sitelist))

C2_SES_microenv_Rsq<- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist) * length(sitelist))

C2_SES_microenv_anova<- vector(mode= "list", length = length(traitlist) * length(sitelist))

l = 1
for (t in 1:length(traitlist)) {
  for(s in 1:length(sitelist)) {
    modeldat <-  C2_microenv_comb |> 
      filter(trait == traitlist[t], 
             site == sitelist[s]) |> 
      drop_na()
    
    
    model<- lme(SES ~ mean_T1_growing_season + mean_moist_growing_season + rock_cover+ mean_soil_depth + STD,
                random = ~1|grid, 
                correlation = corSpher(form = ~ x_coord + y_coord|grid, nugget = TRUE), #spherical structure
                data = modeldat) #only gaussian family possible
    
    
    #Also save results in a list object so we can call it with quarto
    names(C2_SES_microenv_summary)[[l]] <- paste(traitlist[t], sitelist[s], sep = "_")
    C2_SES_microenv_summary[[l]] <- summary(model)
    
    names(C2_SES_microenv_Rsq)[[l]] <- paste(traitlist[t], sitelist[s], sep = "_")
    C2_SES_microenv_Rsq[[l]] <- r.squaredGLMM(model)
    
    names(C2_SES_microenv_anova)[[l]] <- paste(traitlist[t], sitelist[s], sep = "_")
    C2_SES_microenv_anova[[l]] <- anova(model)
    
    l = l+1
    
  }}

```

# Results

`r C5_ele_comb |>  filter(trait == "log_Height") |> drop_na() |> summarise(n = n())` Cells were included in testing how community assembly varies with elevation. `r C5_ele_comb|> filter(trait == "log_Height", site == "GG") |> drop_na() |> summarise(n = n())` Cells were from the low site, `r C5_ele_comb |> filter(trait == "log_Height", site == "WH") |> drop_na() |> summarise(n = n())` cells were from the mid site, and `r C5_ele_comb |> filter(trait == "log_Height", site == "BK") |> drop_na() |> summarise(n = n())` cells were from the high site. Environmental filtering was the dominant assembly mechanism for all traits at all elevations. The C5 null model detected higher than expected trait divergence for plant height and LDMC at the highest elevation (@fig-C5-SES-elevation-ridges), but the C2 null model detected no limiting similarity for any trait at any elevation (@fig-C2-SES-elevation-ridges). Therefore, we conclude that limiting similarity was not driving community assembly at any point on th elevation gradient. Only leaf area followed the trend predicted by the SDH, with environmental filtering becoming stronger with increasing elevation (@fig-C5-SES-elevation-ridges). The environmental filtering of plant height and LDMC became weaker with elevation, while the assembly of SLA showed a hump-shaped relationship with elevation, with environmental filtering being weaker at the mid site than at the low and high site (@fig-C5-SES-elevation-ridges).

Plant height was generally filtered toward shorter plants with elevation, but the diversity of plant height increased with elevation (@fig-RaoQ-elevation-ridges), showing the existence of very short as well as very tall plants in the alpine (@fig-CWM-elevation-ridges) [(Should I put the coefficients and whole model statistics for these models in the appendix? Since it's a separate model for each trait, it feels clumsy to put it in text)]{.underline}. The direction of filtering for leaf area, SLA and LDMC showed a hump shaped relationship with elevation (@fig-CWM-elevation-ridges), with communities at the mid site having larger leaves and less conservative resource-use strategies than at the high and low site.

```{r}
#import trait and abundance data
abun_matrix <-read.csv("All_data/comm_assembly_results/abun_matrix.csv", row.names = 1)

mean_traits <- read.csv("All_data/comm_assembly_results/mean_traits.csv", row.names = 1) |> 
  mutate(log_Height = log(Height_cm), 
         log_LA = log(Leaf_area_mm2), 
         log_LDMC = log(LDMC)) |> #use the same log variables as we do in the models
  select(!c(LDMC, Leaf_area_mm2, Height_cm, Thickness_mm))


#compute CWM of each trait for each cell
library(FD)
cwm <- functcomp(x = mean_traits, a = as.matrix(abun_matrix))
cwm2 <- cwm |>
  rownames_to_column(var = "cellref") |> 
  rename(Cell_ID = cellref)  |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = c("log_Height", "log_LDMC", "log_LA", "SLA"), names_to = "trait", values_to = "cwm_value")

cwm_comb <- pos |> 
  #join, one row in env matches many rows in cell_ses due to it containing ses of different traits
  inner_join(cwm2, by = "Cell_ID", relationship = "one-to-many") 


####model CWM ~ elevation####

names(CWM_ele_cld) = traitlist

for (t in 1:length(traitlist)) {
  modeldat <-  cwm_comb |> 
    filter(trait == traitlist[t]) |> 
    mutate(elevation = as.factor(elevation), 
           grid = as.factor(grid)) |> 
    drop_na()
  
  
  model<- lme(cwm_value ~ elevation ,
                  random = ~1|grid, 
                  correlation = corSpher(form = ~ x_coord + y_coord|grid, nugget = TRUE), #spherical structure
                  data = modeldat) #only gaussian family possible
  
  em_model <- emmeans(model, specs = "elevation", type = "response")
  comp_letters <-cld(em_model, Letters = letters, adjust = "Tukey", sort = FALSE)

  #Also save results in a list object so we can call it with quarto
  CWM_ele_cld[[t]] <- comp_letters
}
```

Micro-environmental factors were weakly related to fine-scale variation in community assembly, with relationships varying between traits and sites. The models had low explanatory power, with R squared values generally below 0.1 (@tbl-R2-models-C5, @tbl-R2-models-C2). Only surface heterogeneity had a somewhat consistent relationship with community assembly, often being related to higher than expected trait divergence (@fig-allsites-microenv_C5_C2), although this relationship was not detected at all sites or for all traits. Other micro-environmental factors had weak and inconsistent effects on community assembly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-allsites-microenv_C5_C2
#| fig-cap: Effects of microenvironmental variables on assembly of traits at the mid site. Coefficients show the effect of microenvironmental variables on the SES calculated with each trait and each null model. Positive coefficients indicate that the variable is related to higher than expected trait divergence, while negative coefficients indicate thet the variable is related to higher than expected trait convergence. Stars indicate significant relationships. 
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| width: 6.5
#| height: 5

#Create tables of coeffieicents for each site, it is easier to manage this way
GG_microenv_results <- expand_grid(null_model = c("C5", "C2"), 
                         trait = c("Height_cm", "Leaf_area_mm2", "LDMC", "SLA"),
                         variable = c("mean soil temperature", "mean soil moisture", "rock cover", "mean soil depth", "surface heterogeneity")) |> 
  mutate(
    coefficient = c(C5_SES_microenv_summary$Height_cm_GG$coefficients$fixed[2:6], 
    C5_SES_microenv_summary$Leaf_area_mm2_GG$coefficients$fixed[2:6], 
    C5_SES_microenv_summary$log_LDMC_GG$coefficients$fixed[2:6], 
    C5_SES_microenv_summary$SLA_GG$coefficients$fixed[2:6],
    C2_SES_microenv_summary$Height_cm_GG$coefficients$fixed[2:6], 
    C2_SES_microenv_summary$Leaf_area_mm2_GG$coefficients$fixed[2:6], 
    C2_SES_microenv_summary$log_LDMC_GG$coefficients$fixed[2:6], 
    C2_SES_microenv_summary$SLA_GG$coefficients$fixed[2:6]), 

    std_error = c(C5_SES_microenv_summary$Height_cm_GG$tTable[2:6,2], 
    C5_SES_microenv_summary$Leaf_area_mm2_GG$tTable[2:6,2], 
    C5_SES_microenv_summary$log_LDMC_GG$tTable[2:6,2], 
    C5_SES_microenv_summary$SLA_GG$tTable[2:6,2],
    C2_SES_microenv_summary$Height_cm_GG$tTable[2:6,2], 
    C2_SES_microenv_summary$Leaf_area_mm2_GG$tTable[2:6,2], 
    C2_SES_microenv_summary$log_LDMC_GG$tTable[2:6,2], 
    C2_SES_microenv_summary$SLA_GG$tTable[2:6,2])) |>  
    mutate(
    lower_ci = coefficient - 1.96*std_error, 
    upper_ci = coefficient + 1.96*std_error)

#bind all tabes together
allsites_microenv <- bind_rows(GG_microenv_results, WH_microenv_results, BK_microenv_results) |> 
  mutate(site = c(rep("low", nrow(GG_microenv_results)), rep("mid", nrow(WH_microenv_results)), rep("high", nrow(BK_microenv_results))), 
         site = factor(site, levels = c("low", "mid", "high"))) |> 
  mutate(sign = if_else(lower_ci < 0 & upper_ci > 0," ", "*")) |> 
  relocate(sign, .after = variable)

write.csv(allsites_microenv, "All_data/comm_assembly_results/SES_microenv_model_results_table.csv")


l1 <- c("Height_cm" = "Height", "SLA" = "SLA", "LDMC" = "LDMC", "Leaf_area_mm2" = "LA", "low" = "low", "mid" = "mid", "high" = "high")
allsites_microenv_plot <- allsites_microenv |>

            show.legend = FALSE)+
  facet_grid(site~trait,
             labeller = as_labeller(l1, default = label_parsed)) +
```

# Discussion

Some preliminary ideas:

Environmental filtering dominant assembly mechanism, not consistently increasing in strength with elevation. Mid site shows unexpected deviation to less conservative, larger leafed species. This could be due to relaxation of environmental filters here, or because of strong competition selecting for more acquisitive (competitive?) traits.

Micro-environmental variables only weakly influence community assembly, and do not have consistent effects. This suggests that assembly at this scale is largely neutral, despite large differences in micro-environmental conditions?

Perhaps missing: An analysis or figure showing the extent of environmental variation present here?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-validation-results
#| tbl-cap: Cross validation results from inverse-distance-weighted interpolation of the mean soil moisture and mean soil temperature of the growing season. Grid number is the unique ID of each grid in each site.Number of loggers are the number of TMS loggers used to create the interpolated temperature or moisture surface. $R^2$ is the squared Pearson correlation coefficient between the observed and interpolated temperature or moisture value. The root mean square error is the square root of the mean squared difference between observed and interpolated values in the grid. The bias is the mean of the differences between observed and interpolated values in the grid.
#| message: false
#| echo: false

#import validation results
validation_results <- read.csv("All_data/clean_data/Environmental data/Imke_microclimate_indices_interpolation_validation.csv")

validation_grid <- validation_results |> 
  group_by(site, grid_number, variable) |> 
  summarise(
    n        = n(),
    R2       = ifelse(var(observed) > 0, 
                      cor(observed, predicted)^2, NA_real_),
    RMSE     = sqrt(mean(error^2)),
    bias     = mean(error),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) |> 
  mutate(site = case_when(site == "BK" ~ "high", 
                          site == "WH" ~ "mid", 
                          site == "GG" ~ "low"), 
         site = factor(site, levels = c("low", "mid", "high")), 
         variable = case_when(variable == "mean_T1_growing_season" ~ "mean soil temperature", 
                              variable == "mean_moist_growing_season" ~ "mean soil moisture")) |> 
  arrange(variable, site, grid_number) |> 
  flextable() |> 
  colformat_double(j = 4:6, digits = 3) |> 
  set_header_labels(site = "Site", 
                    grid_number = "Grid number", 
                    variable = "Variable", 
                    n = "Number of loggers", 
                    R2 = "R\u00B2", 
                    RMSE = "Root mean square error", 
                    bias = "Bias") |> 
  align(j = 1:6, align = "center", part = "all") |>
  theme_vanilla() |> 
  bold(part = "header") |> 
  autofit() |> 
  fit_to_width(max_width = 6.5)

validation_grid
```
